name: NAU Washington Elm

location.address: In front of Old Main, Northern Arizona University, Flagstaff, AZ 86011

official_register.name: Arizona's Magnificent Trees (Witness/Heritage Tree AZ0022 'American Elm', nominated by NAU, 2011)

access: Free, open at any time: on the lawn of the open NAU campus, in front of Old Main.
transport: NAU campus is about 1.5 km south-east of downtown Flagstaff; Mountain Line buses stop at the campus; about 20 minutes on foot from the Amtrak station

location_site.name: Lawn in front of Old Main, NAU

how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the two plaques at its base, one from the Daughters of the American Revolution and one from the Arizona centennial programme. It stands on the lawn in front of Old Main.
story:
This elm was planted in 1931 and is, officially, a witness to Arizona's statehood in 1912. Its two plaques do not quite agree. The older one, from the Coconino Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, records that on 22 April 1931 the chapter gave the Arizona State Teachers College at Flagstaff a sprig of the Washington Elm of Cambridge, Massachusetts, the tree under which George Washington is said to have taken command of the Continental Army. The newer plaque, from 2012, names it an Arizona Centennial Witness Tree, alive from 1912 to 2012. A tree planted in 1931 cannot have stood in 1912; that wording belongs to the centennial programme, not to the tree.

The Cambridge story deserves its own caveat. The idea that Washington took command beneath that elm has itself been called a legend, so treat this tree's ancestry as the plaque tells it.

The teachers college became Northern Arizona University, and the elm has stood in front of Old Main for about 95 years. Around 2011 the university reported it sick with European elm scale, and the DAR chapter gave a thousand dollars toward its treatment. We have not seen a recent report on its health, so if you pass, tell us how it looks.
